markdown.markdown:
From the previous class, the equation of motion for a 1-DOF **undamped** system is: $$m\ddot{u}(t) + ku(t) = 0$$ and its general solution is: $$u(t) = \frac{v_0}{\omega_n\cos\phi}\,\sin\!\left(\omega_n t + \phi\right), \qquad \phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{u_0\,\omega_n}{v_0}\right), \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$ where $u_0 = u(0)$ is the initial displacement and $v_0 = \dot{u}(0)$ is the initial velocity. The system oscillates **indefinitely** at $\omega_n$, since there is no energy dissipation. --- ## 3.1 The Forced Undamped System A real structure is rarely left to vibrate freely. It is typically **driven** by some external force. The simplest and most important case is a **harmonic excitation**: $$F(t) = F_0 \sin(\omega t)$$ where $F_0$ is the force amplitude and $\omega$ is the **excitation frequency**. The equation of motion becomes: $$\boxed{m\ddot{u}(t) + ku(t) = F_0\sin(\omega t)}$$ ::: {.callout-warning} ## Do not confuse $\omega$ and $\omega_n$ $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$ is the **natural frequency** — a property of the system. $\omega$ is the **excitation frequency** — a property of the loading. We can choose $\omega$ freely. ::: ### Solution Structure From differential equations theory, the **complete solution** is the sum of two parts: $$u(t) = \underbrace{u_h(t)}_{\substack{\text{free / natural}\\\text{response}}} + \underbrace{u_p(t)}_{\substack{\text{forced / particular}\\\text{response}}}$$ From the previous class, the natural response is: $$u_h(t) = A\sin(\omega_n t + \phi)$$ For the forced response, we **propose** a particular solution of the form: $$u_p(t) = U\sin(\omega t)$$ Since there is no damping, both components persist indefinitely: they sum to give the **complete behavior** of the system. --- ## 3.2 Finding the Forced Harmonic Response Starting from $m\ddot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)$, substitute the trial $u_p(t) = U\sin(\omega t)$: $$\dot{u}_p(t) = U\omega\cos(\omega t), \qquad \ddot{u}_p(t) = -U\omega^2\sin(\omega t)$$ Substituting into the equation of motion: $$m\bigl(-U\omega^2\bigr)\sin(\omega t) + kU\sin(\omega t) = F_0\sin(\omega t)$$ Dividing through by $\sin(\omega t)$: $$-mU\omega^2 + kU = F_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad U(k - m\omega^2) = F_0$$ $$\boxed{U = \frac{F_0}{k - m\omega^2}}$$ Dividing numerator and denominator by $k$ and using $k/m = \omega_n^2$: $$\boxed{U = \frac{F_0/k}{1 - \left(\dfrac{\omega}{\omega_n}\right)^2}}$$ The quantity $F_0/k$ is the **static deflection** — the displacement under a static force $F_0$. ### Case 1: $\omega < \omega_n$ $$\omega_n^2 - \omega^2 > 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad U > 0$$ The particular response is $u_p(t) = U\sin(\omega t)$: force $F(t)$ and response $u_p(t)$ point in the **same direction**. $$\longrightarrow F(t) \qquad \longrightarrow u_p(t)$$ ### Case 2: $\omega > \omega_n$ $$\omega_n^2 - \omega^2 < 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad U < 0$$ Writing $U = -|U|$: $$u_p(t) = -|U|\sin(\omega t) = |U|\sin(\omega t + \pi)$$ Force and response point in **opposite directions** — the mass moves against the force. $$\longrightarrow F(t) \qquad \longleftarrow u_p(t)$$ ### Phase Shift at $\omega = \omega_n$ As $\omega$ crosses $\omega_n$, the denominator changes sign and the phase **jumps discontinuously** from 0° to 180°: $$\text{Phase} = \begin{cases} 0° & \omega < \omega_n \\ 180° & \omega > \omega_n \end{cases}$$ ### Why Does This Shift Happen? Substituting $u_p$ back into the equation of motion: $$m\ddot{u}_p + ku_p = U\,(k - m\omega^2)\sin(\omega t)$$ The bracket $k - m\omega^2$ changes sign at $\omega = \omega_n$: - For $\omega < \omega_n$: the **stiffness** $k$ dominates — the system is *stiffness-controlled*. - For $\omega > \omega_n$: the **inertia** $m\omega^2$ dominates — the system is *mass-controlled*, and the sign of $U$ flips. --- ## 3.3 Introduction to Damped Systems Systems without damping are an idealization. **Real structures dissipate energy** through viscous friction, internal material damping, dry friction (Coulomb), and other mechanisms. Adding damping makes the model **physically realistic** and, crucially, removes the singularity at resonance. The forced equation of motion for a **damped** system is: $$m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)$$ where the double underline on $c\dot{u}$ reminds us this is the new term. ### Why Does Damping Require a Cosine Term? In the undamped case, a pure sine $u_p = U\sin(\omega t)$ worked as a particular solution. With damping, however, the $c\dot{u}$ term introduces a component proportional to $\cos(\omega t)$. Therefore, we must try a **two-component** particular solution: $$u_p(t) = A\sin(\omega t) + B\cos(\omega t)$$ > The cosine term $B\cos(\omega t)$ represents the **90°-delayed** part of the response that only exists because of damping. If $c = 0$, we will find $B = 0$ and recover the undamped result. ### Setting Up the Algebra Computing derivatives: $$\dot{u}_p = A\omega\cos(\omega t) - B\omega\sin(\omega t)$$ $$\ddot{u}_p = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t) - B\omega^2\cos(\omega t)$$ Substituting into the equation of motion and grouping terms by $\sin(\omega t)$ and $\cos(\omega t)$: **For** $\sin(\omega t)$: $$A(k - m\omega^2) - cB\omega = F_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \alpha = F_0$$ **For** $\cos(\omega t)$: $$B(k - m\omega^2) + cA\omega = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \beta = 0$$ Let us define $D = k - m\omega^2$ for convenience. Then: $$\begin{cases} AD - cB\omega = F_0 \\ BD + cA\omega = 0 \end{cases}$$ Solving this $2\times 2$ system (details shown in Class 4): $$A = \frac{F_0(k-m\omega^2)}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}, \qquad B = \frac{-F_0 c\omega}{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}$$ The **physical amplitude** and **phase** of the response are: $$U = \sqrt{A^2+B^2} = \frac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}}, \qquad \phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{c\omega}{k-m\omega^2}\right)$$ The complete derivation and the dimensionless form are covered in Class 4. --- ## 🎛️ Interactive: Forced Undamped Response Explorer Use the sliders to explore directly the equations derived above. We introduced damping but did not finish the derivation. Increasing $k$ or decreasing $m$ shifts $\omega_n$ to the right. ����������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������� --- ## What Comes Next In this class we found the forced undamped response and saw that resonance causes unbounded amplitude when $\omega = \omega_n$. We introduced damping but did not finish the derivation. In Class 4 we complete the solution for the **damped** forced response: $$m\ddot{u} + c\dot{u} + ku = F_0\sin(\omega t)$$ and introduce the **dimensionless form** — a single pair of curves that describes every possible 1-DOF system, regardless of the specific values of $m$, $k$, $c$, or $F_0$.
